We calculate the hourly VRE difference, find the median ratio between the two datasets, and adjust the net load by subtracting the SERVM VRE amount divided by this ratio. This creates a net load aligned with our VRE assumptions. ● Calculating Price per Load Unit: We divide the average monthly wholesale price by the ACC’s net load for NP-15 (PGE’s hourly net load) and SP-15 (SCE and SDGE’s hourly net load) for each month and hour, creating a unit price. ● Generating New Wholesale Prices: We multiply the unit price by our hourly net load for each month and hour in NP-15 and SP-15, resulting in new, adjusted wholesale prices. ● Applying the Prices: The new NP-15 prices become PGE's 2030 wholesale prices, while the new SP-15 prices are used for SDGE and SCE in 2030. 2.3 End use load response models A novel set of end use load response models were developed for this study. The end-uses studied here are space cooling, space heating, water heating, crop irrigation, pool and spa pumps, and electric vehicle (EV) charging, all for both residential and commercial applications, except for crop irrigation. In general, these load models take in an expected baseline electricity 11 demand profile and a price signal and determine the load response. Ultimately, three different modeling approaches are used, as shown in Figure 4. The thermal load shift model considers the baseline demand profile as an hourly service requirement that must be met and accordingly accounts for the duration of the load shift and extra energy required to make up for losses. The “fully dispatchable load” model (applied to pumping and EV loads) assumes the baseline demand to be completely flexible during a given time period, assuming that the total baseline electricity demand is met. Finally, more detailed EV simulation modeling and stationary battery system modeling leverages an existing tool to optimize operation of these devices according to price signals and, in the case of EVs, assumed energetic demand for driving. These models operate on an hourly basis for a one-year time period, with the exception of some of the supplementary EV simulation modeling that is done on a 15-minute basis. Hourly results can be converted to smaller time increments by linearly interpolating between the hourly values; these are likely to be quite close to results based on actual more fine-grained prices. Figure 4. Overview of end use response models Each end use response model calculates the hourly load impact of the price response. This price response can be multiplied by the hourly price to give the bill savings or can be multiplied by other weights to calculate different metrics for describing the load response.
